She said she would come by coach.
He asked me if I had slept.
She explained that she was tired.
He promised he would come back the next day.
She told me not to worry.
To apply the sequence of tenses after a verb in the past (il a dit que…).
To shift: présent → imparfait, passé composé → plus-que-parfait, futur → conditionnel.
To change time expressions: demain → le lendemain, hier → la veille, aujourd’hui → ce jour-là.
To report questions and orders in the past (il a demandé si…, elle m’a dit de…).
To talk about the first days with a newborn.

Saturday, 6 March. The grandmother arrived by coach yesterday. This morning, Julien and Radu are in the kitchen, exhausted after a sleepless night. Radu tells Julien what he talked about with his grandmother at the coach station.
So, tell me. What did she say to you at the coach station?
First, she told me she hadn’t slept the whole journey. She explained that she had talked to the driver for thirty hours.
Then she asked me if the baby was healthy, if Ioana was all right, and if you had cried.
I told her everyone was fine, and that you had cried more than the baby.
She said it was normal, and that my grandfather had cried for three days when my mother was born.
And what next? How long is she going to stay?
She announced that she would stay a month. She said she would take care of the cooking, the cleaning and the nights, and that you would finally be able to sleep.
I told her. She answered that she had raised four children without a washing machine or disposable nappies, and that she didn’t need anybody’s advice.
(he laughs) I love her. And last night, it’s true, Rose-Hélène slept for four hours in a row for the first time.
Because Granny rocked her singing Romanian songs. She told me yesterday she would teach her Romanian even before she could talk.
And did she ask you anything else?
(he blushes) Yes. She asked me who “the pretty Spanish girl” was that Mum had told her about on the phone. And she told me to invite her to dinner on Sunday. She promised she would make sarmale.
not … had (“elle n’avait pas dormi” = she hadn’t slept)
had (“elle avait parlé” = she had talked)
was going (“allait bien” = was all right)
goes (“elle va rester” = she’s going to stay)
“Kel vyẽ-dreh”: the conditional ends in an open “e”, like the imparfait.
“Kee-la-veh fee-nee”: linked, with liaison on l.
“Nwee blãsh”: a night without sleep. A very common expression among parents!
“O-keh”: the h is aspirated, so no elision: “le hoquet” (not “l’hoquet”).

In chapter 28 you learnt reported speech with the reporting verb in the PRESENT (elle dit que…). When the reporting verb is in the PAST (elle a dit que…, il a répondu que…), the tenses in the reported clause “move” one step back into the past:
Elle a dit qu’elle était fatiguée.
Elle a dit qu’elle avait dormi.
Elle a dit qu’elle resterait un mois.
Elle a dit qu’elle allait partir.
Elle a dit qu’elle était jeune.

English does the same backshift (“she said she was tired”, “she said she would stay”), but Romanian doesn’t (“A zis că e obosită”). In French it is compulsory: “Elle a dit qu’elle ÉTAIT fatiguée”, “qu’elle RESTERAIT”. It’s one of the most important B1 rules.
When you tell the story later, “today” is no longer today. The expressions change too:
Example: « Je reviendrai demain. » → Il a promis qu’il reviendrait le lendemain.
3. Questions and orders in the past
She asked me if the baby was healthy.
She asked me who the pretty Spanish girl was.
He asked me what I had answered.
She told me to invite her on Sunday.
For orders: dire DE + infinitive. “Elle m’a dit de l’inviter” (not “que je l’invite”, which is possible but heavier).
So you don’t keep repeating “il a dit”, use more precise verbs:
Elle a expliqué qu’elle avait parlé avec le chauffeur.
Il a répondu que tout allait bien.
Elle a annoncé qu’elle resterait un mois.
Elle a promis qu’elle ferait des sarmale.
Il a avoué qu’il avait pleuré.
Elle a ajouté que c’était normal.
Il s’est plaint qu’il n’avait pas dormi.

The following Sunday, Lucia arrived at seven o’clock sharp, with a bunch of tulips for Ioana, a little cloth rabbit for Rose-Hélène, and a box of turrón, Spanish nougat, for the grandmother. Radu had advised her not to forget anything. He had added that his grandmother noticed everything.

Lucia was more nervous than before her architecture exam. She had asked Radu what his grandmother liked, what she hated, and whether she should kiss her on the cheek. Radu had answered that she liked people who ate a lot, that she hated people who ate little, and that she should give her three kisses, not two.

When the door opened, the grandmother was there, in her flowery apron. She looked Lucia up and down, for a long time, in silence. Lucia smiled, said “Bună seara” with an adorable Spanish accent, and kissed her three times.

The grandmother turned to Ioana and said something in Romanian. Ioana translated: “She says you have beautiful eyes, and that you’re too thin.” Lucia laughed. She replied that in Spain her grandmother used to tell her exactly the same thing.

Dinner began. On the table there were sarmale, of course, but also a ciorbă, plăcinte and an enormous walnut cake. The grandmother had been cooking since the morning. She had refused to let anyone help her, even Ioana. She had said it was her exam too.

During the meal, the grandmother asked questions. Lots of questions. Ioana translated, and Radu got redder and redder. She asked Lucia where she came from, what her parents did, whether she went to church, how many brothers and sisters she had, and whether she could cook.

Lucia answered everything calmly. She explained that she came from Salamanca, that her father was a teacher and her mother a nurse, that she had two younger brothers, and that she went to mass with her grandmother when she went home to Spain. As for cooking, she admitted that she could only make one thing: her grandfather’s potato tortilla.

The grandmother nodded, without saying anything. Then she asked one more thing. Ioana hesitated before translating. “She’s asking whether you really love her grandson, or whether it’s just an Erasmus fling.”
There was a long silence. Radu dropped his fork. Julien looked at his plate. Rose-Hélène, in her cot, made a little noise, as if to say that she too was waiting for the answer.

Lucia put down her knife and fork. She looked the grandmother straight in the eyes and spoke slowly, so that Ioana could translate everything. She said that at first she had thought it would be a story of a few months. That she hadn’t wanted to fall in love, because she knew the Erasmus would end one day. But that she had understood, the evening Radu got lost outside the residence, that she had never met anyone so funny and so kind.
She added that she had spoken to her parents the week before, and that she had told them she wanted to do her master’s in Lyon the following year. To stay near him.
Radu opened his mouth. He hadn’t known. Nobody had. He looked at Lucia as if he were seeing her for the first time.

The grandmother said nothing for a long moment. Then she stood up, walked round the table, and took Lucia’s face in both hands, exactly as she had done with Ioana in Iași, on the night of the wedding. She said a sentence in Romanian, very softly.

Ioana had tears in her eyes. “She says you’ve passed the exam. And that she’ll teach you to make sarmale before she goes back to Romania. Because a woman who loves her grandson must know how to make them.”
Lucia burst out laughing and crying at the same time. Radu stood up to take her in his arms. And the grandmother, satisfied, went back to her seat and filled Lucia’s plate with four more sarmale.

Later, while Lucia was helping Ioana with the washing-up, Radu asked his grandmother, in Romanian, what she really thought. She told him she had known from the doorway. He asked her how. She said she had seen the way Lucia had looked at the baby, and then the way she had looked at him, Radu. And that she had seen exactly the same thing, sixty years earlier, in the eyes of her Ion.

That evening, walking Lucia back to the residence, Radu asked her why she hadn’t told him about the master’s. She answered that she had wanted to be sure first. And that she had needed the approval of someone very important. “My grandmother’s?” asked Radu. “No,” answered Lucia, laughing. “Victor’s. He slept on my lap all through dinner. I think that’s a yes.”

The sarmale lesson took place the following Thursday. The grandmother had announced that it would take a whole afternoon, and that she would speak only Romanian, because, according to her, sarmale didn’t understand French. Lucia wrote everything down in a little notebook: the Romanian words on the left, the gestures on the right.

At the end, the kitchen looked like a battlefield, but Lucia’s sarmale were almost round. The grandmother tasted one, slowly. Then she declared that they were better than Radu’s. Radu protested that he had never made any. She answered that that was exactly why.

In the evening, in the baby’s diary, Ioana wrote: “My little Rose-Hélène, today your family grew again. Nobody said it out loud, but everyone understood. One day I’ll tell you how a Spanish girl won over a Romanian grandmother with three kisses and a tortilla.”

“And I,” she added on the last line, “promised your great-grandmother that I would send her a photo of you every Sunday, once she had gone back to Romania. She answered that she would show them to the whole village. I think she really will.”
kiss on the cheek (“faire la bise”)
knees (“sur mes genoux” = on my lap)

After a week, Ioana writes in the baby’s diary what the visitors said. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
11 March. My little Rose-Hélène, you’re a week old. I’d like to write down here everything people said when they saw you for the first time.
Your grandfather Pierre said you had his mother’s nose, and that you would be a baker. Your grandmother Brigitte answered that you would rather be a singer, like your aunt Manon.
Madame Bernard explained that she had seen thousands of babies, but that she had never seen one so calm. She added that it was surely thanks to the music.
Sophie brought you a little heart-shaped brioche. She said it would be your first cake, but that you would have to wait six months to taste it. Your daddy ate it for you.
Karim and Leïla came with their daughter, who asked if you could talk yet. When I told her you couldn’t, she promised she would teach you all the words she knew.
Your Romanian grandmother said you were the most beautiful baby she had ever seen. Then she admitted she had said the same thing about me, about Radu, and about all her grandchildren.

And Hélène? Hélène said almost nothing. She held you in her arms for an hour, and at the end she whispered that she could now leave in peace. I told her not to talk nonsense. She laughed, and promised she would stay a long time yet.
